1.pericope_label: Jesus walked in Galilee, for the Jews sought to kill him: My time is not yet come

schools.summary: Augustine makes the withdrawal a precedent, since the Head hid first so that no guilt attaches to a member who hides later, and holds that Christ could have escaped had he chosen, the retreat being an accommodation to our weakness; he reads “my time” of the time of glory where the brethren’s, the glory of the world, is always ready, bids the Lord’s body answer its insulters that our country is lofty and the way to it low, finds in their seeking human glory for him the proof that they did not believe, and takes the brethren for Mary’s kindred and not her offspring, the womb that bore the Lord conceiving no other as the sepulchre held no other. Bede paraphrases their advice as a summons to the royal city, where the rulers might see his miracles and praise follow.

Chrysostom has him flee as man and remain as God, admires Evangelists who report what tells against their Master, and finds bitterness under the courtesy, since the charge that nobody acts in secret taxes him with fear while the clause about being known taxes him with vain glory; he suspects the brethren of meaning to betray him, so that the time refused is the time of the cross, and notes that the world cannot hate men of its own mind. Theophylact says the disciples meant are the multitudes.

Barnes limits the plot to the rulers, the people never having attempted his life, and has Christ wait until the crowds had passed lest it be said he chose his moment to raise a tumult; he and Ellicott both report Josephus calling tabernacles the greatest of the feasts, Ellicott adding that it was a memorial of the deliverance and a harvest thanksgiving, and calling the “yet” doubtful and needless, since on the better reading it is never said he went up to the feast at all, only that he refused to go as they meant it, openly with the caravan. Lightfoot lays out the month of Tisri day by day, down to the high priest sequestered seven days before the Atonement to rehearse the rites, and holds that Christ denies the time and not the going. Robertson keeps the plain negative and finds the manner of verse ten exactly opposite to the advice.

Calvin makes the withdrawal a rule for danger, that it is not ours to ask what God has decreed but what he commands, and warns that we must not for the sake of life lose the reasons for living; he ends on the murmuring, where the one Church then on earth appears a shapeless chaos whose rulers hold the people by fear. Gill reads the booths as a type of Christ tabernacling in human nature and an emblem of the saints dwelling in the tabernacles of their bodies.

Clarke supplies the ritual in full — branches of palm and willow bound with gold and silver cords, the daily circuit of the altar with Hosanna and trumpets, the sevenfold circuit called the great Hosanna, and water drawn from Siloam and poured with wine while the people sang of the wells of salvation — and ties it forward to the cry of the last day; he then raises Porphyry’s charge of falsehood, that Christ said he would not go and went, and answers that he said only not yet.

Henry marks the verb, that it is not said he durst not but that he would not, and adds that providence may cast men of merit into obscurity as it did his Master, who even so walked rather than sat still; that divine institutions do not go out of date, though John calls it the feast of the Jews because it was shortly to be abolished; and that the kindred had honour but not a saving honour, since grace runs in no blood — their fault being presumption in prescribing to Christ, carelessness of his safety, and self at the bottom.

debates.question: Did “I go not up yet unto this feast” make the later going a falsehood?

positions.view: No — he denied the time, not the going, which answers Porphyry’s charge
The “yet” is a doubtful and needless reading; on the better text he never says he will not go to the feast, only that he will not go as they meant it, openly with the caravan
Keep the plain negative, and read verse ten as a manner exactly opposite to their advice
Mary’s kindred and not her offspring, the womb that bore the Lord conceiving no other
Kindred with real honour but no saving honour, since grace runs in no blood

outliers.claim: Suspects the brethren of meaning to betray him, so that the time he refuses is the time of the cross rather than a time of festival safety.

themes: After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.
Now the Jews’ feast of tabernacles was at hand.
His brethren therefore said unto him, Depart hence, and go into Judea, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest.
For there is no man that doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, shew thyself to the world.
For neither did his brethren believe in him.
Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready.
The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil.
Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come.
When he had said these words unto them, he abode still in Galilee.
But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.
Then the Jews sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he?
And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.
Howbeit no man spake openly of him for fear of the Jews.

14.pericope_label: How knoweth this man letters, having never learned? My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me

schools.summary: Augustine makes the timing fulfil the earlier refusal exactly, and adds that he went up not to the feast but to the light, his own feast day being the one his passion made; he resolves “not mine” by identity, since the Father’s teaching is his Word and Christ is that Word, so the doctrine is at once his and not his, against the Sabellian heresy which makes Father and Son two names for one thing. He makes doing the will mean believing, and lays down that we must not seek to understand in order to believe but believe in order to understand; he has Moses convict them, the law of the eighth day overriding the law of the seventh, since circumcision signs salvation and no man may rest from that work, and observes that the caster-out of devils was told he had one. Bede takes the answer for an example, that a wrong censure is better met by wholesome advice than by asserting a truth one could assert. Alcuin gives three reasons for the rite and says it then had the virtue baptism has now, only the gate was not yet open.

Chrysostom explains the delay as calculated, since men who had hunted for him would attend the more closely when he appeared without warning, and says it was not the doctrine they admired but something else altogether; he divides “not mine” differently from Augustine, his as he taught it and not his as it came from the Father, finding in the denial the strongest proof that the two are one, and reduces the test to a condition — put away the anger and envy you bear me and nothing will hinder the knowing. On the charges he answers the first from the commandment: the law says thou shalt not kill, and they seek to kill; if he broke a law it healed a man, where they transgress for an evil end.

Barnes works the promise out as evidence, internal and of two kinds, claims that only men who wish to live in sin doubt, and adds that God’s goodness put this proof within every man’s reach, since it takes no great learning to be a Christian. Ellicott puts the stress on the willing, which precedes faith, rather than the deed, which follows, insists the “any man” excludes nobody, naming Saul the Pharisee, Cornelius and Justin, and draws the circumcision argument a fortiori: if a patriarchal rite overrides the Mosaic sabbath because the fathers came before Moses, an act of love must override it the more, being older than all time. Robertson quotes Westcott, that where there is no sympathy there can be no understanding, and presses it further, that unbelieving critics are disqualified as witnesses, their isolation proving nothing about God. Lightfoot shows the rabbis themselves ruling that circumcision and its cure null the sabbath, while disputing whether a stranger’s son might be so circumcised.
Calvin says sound judgment flows from the fear of God, so that men unable to tell truth from falsehood want the first requisite, which is piety.
Clarke supplies the retort, that men who ask why the healing was not deferred to a working day should be asked why the circumcising is not.

Henry adds that the people would be freer after days in their booths, that he came when friends and enemies alike had stopped looking, and that the teaching shamed the priests by taking their office out of their hands; on the learning he notes that Moses was taught the wisdom of Egypt while Christ was not taught even that of the Jews, and that a learned age was chosen lest the religion look like a design to impose on the world.

debates.question: How can the doctrine be both his and not his?

positions.view: By identity — the Father’s teaching is his Word, and Christ is that Word
By aspect — his as he taught it, not his as it came from the Father, the denial itself proving the two are one

debates.question: What does “if any man will do his will” require?

positions.view: Believing, so that we believe in order to understand and not the reverse
The removal of anger and envy, after which nothing hinders the knowing
The willing, which precedes faith, rather than the deed, which follows
A reachable proof: internal evidence of two kinds, since it takes no great learning to be a Christian

outliers.claim: Turns the promise into a rule of evidence against the critics, holding that unbelieving scholarship is disqualified as a witness because it lacks the sympathy understanding requires.

themes: Now about the midst of the feast Jesus went up into the temple, and taught.
And the Jews marvelled, saying, How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?
Jesus answered them, and said, My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.
If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
He that speaketh of himself seeketh his own glory: but he that seeketh his glory that sent him, the same is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me?
The people answered and said, Thou hast a devil: who goeth about to kill thee?
Jesus answered and said unto them, I have done one work, and ye all marvel.
Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; (not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man.
If a man on the sabbath day receive circumcision, that the law of Moses should not be broken; are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day?
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

25.pericope_label: Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ? I am not come of myself

schools.summary: Augustine reads secrecy and boldness together, since he went up hidden to show figuratively that he was hidden even in the feast the Jews kept, and now the power appears which had been taken for timidity; he adds that, not understanding that power, they supposed the rulers’ knowledge was what spared him. He allows their expectation a foundation, since the Scriptures say both things, foretelling whence Christ should come as man while hiding him as God from the profane, and takes “we know whence he is” as true and false at once: they knew Jesus of Nazareth and his parents, the birth from the Virgin being the only part hidden from them.

Chrysostom makes something of the note that these were men of Jerusalem, where the miracles had been most and the people were worst, ready to surrender every judgment to corrupt rulers, and asks whether it was not itself a miracle that men who had raged for his life stood suddenly quiet.

Lightfoot asks how the expectation agrees with the later verse about Bethlehem and answers that they looked for a manifestation there, then a hiding, then a second appearing from nobody knew where, quoting the Midrash on the roe that appears and is hidden with Moses as the pattern. Barnes gives the same sources, crediting Lightfoot, and finds the notion corrected where men are told not to go out to the desert after a Christ. Robertson hears contempt in the demonstrative, agrees the concession about his origin is terse and real, has Christ pass the popular theology by to charge them with ignorance of the Father, and keeps the imperfect of the arrest as a seeking begun rather than finished. Ellicott marks how a technical reason, never examined, was enough to stifle every growing conviction and annul all his words and works; he grants a real concession, those features being known to friend and foe alike, while pressing that an outer life tells little even of a brother man, insists the word rendered true means not truthful but the ideally existent One, bases the claim to know the Father on oneness of essence and a true mission, and separates cause from occasion in the failed arrest — nobody laid a hand on him because the crowd was divided, while the hour not yet come is the writer’s primary cause, the beloved disciple having learned, looking back from old age, that every deed of that life had its hour mapped in the counsels of God.

Calvin makes “we know whence he is” irony, that they know everything and know nothing, and adds that there is no more destructive plague than men intoxicated by the little knowledge they have; he declines to press the clauses about the Father as far as Ellicott does, allowing a heavenly descent to be inferred but denying it would prove eternal divinity against the Arians, and takes a warning for teachers from it, that a man who has truly ascertained the truth of God may boldly resist all men, as Jeremiah appealed when charged with imposture, but that we must beware of fanatics who give out their own inventions as oracles.

Clarke traces the expectation instead to the question who shall declare his generation, remarks that the miraculous conception would have relieved them, quotes with Robertson the rabbinic proverb that three things come unlooked for — a thing found by chance, the sting of a scorpion and the Messiah — would read “ye both know me” as a question, taking them on their own profession and then adding what they lack, that he is no self-authorised prophet, and notes a variant turning “I am” into “I came”, judging it slight and too refined. Wesley divides the clauses to answer the two questions, generation to whence and mission to who.

debates.question: Where did the expectation that Christ’s origin would be unknown come from?

positions.view: From a rabbinic scheme of manifestation, hiding and second appearing, documented in the Midrash on the roe
From “who shall declare his generation”, a difficulty the miraculous conception would have relieved
From Scripture itself, which foretells his human origin while hiding his divine one from the profane

debates.question: How is “ye both know me, and ye know whence I am” to be taken?

positions.view: True and false at once — they knew Nazareth and the parents, not the Virgin birth
Irony: they know everything and know nothing
A question, granting their profession before adding what they lack
A real concession about the outer life, which tells little even of a brother man

outliers.claim: Refuses to argue eternal divinity from this passage against the Arians, allowing only that a heavenly descent may be inferred — a deliberate restraint where Ellicott reads oneness of essence.

themes: Then said some of them of Jerusalem, Is not this he, whom they seek to kill?
But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?
Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
Then cried Jesus in the temple as he taught, saying, Ye both know me, and ye know whence I am: and I am not come of myself, but he that sent me is true, whom ye know not.
But I know him: for I am from him, and he hath sent me.
Then they sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come.

31.pericope_label: The Pharisees sent officers to take him: ye shall seek me, and shall not find me

schools.summary: Augustine has the physician gather the poor and humble, who saw their infirmities soonest and took his medicine without hesitation, and reads their question as meaning that if there are not two Christs then this is he; unable to find the officers taking him against his will, he has them sent to hear him teach instead, and puts the answer about going as meaning that what they wish to do now they will do in time, but not now, because it is not his will. Bede takes the going for a return to the Father at whose command he became incarnate, from which he has never come back.

Chrysostom will not call the people’s faith sound, since their form of words shows they were not steady in believing him the Christ, and adds that grosser minds are moved by miracles and not doctrine; he notes that he had taught often before without being so handled, that the praise of the crowd stung the rulers though the sabbath was still the charge they named, and that being afraid to act themselves they sent others. In the answer he hears the greatest humility, as though Christ asked why they made such haste and bade them wait a little, and marks that he does not say “I am here” but “I am with you”, since persecution would not stop his teaching them the way of salvation; on the seeking that would fail he looks to the women who lamented him and to the taking of the city. Theophylact hears a threat of complaint to the Father, an injury to the sent being an injury to the sender.

Barnes dwells on the love of it, that the offer of salvation was made to his own persecutors while they were seeking his life, reads the seeking that fails of the Messiah rather than of Jesus — a nation in its calamities desiring a deliverer and being disappointed — keeps to Jews scattered in every land, and observes that no answer was returned, the question of place being turned aside for their own salvation. Robertson glosses the verb of going as a withdrawing and calls the saying enigmatic to those who heard it. Lightfoot takes “the dispersed among the Gentiles” in its strict sense of Greeks and leaves open whether the dispersed Greeks or the Jews among them are meant, both being the most scattered nations under heaven, the key lying in the distinction between Hebrews and Hellenists. Ellicott agrees the better manuscripts omit the pronoun but takes the hearers to be the hierarchy at large, calls the guess at his destination another instance of men unable to read any meaning off the surface, and traces the dispersion to three centres — Babylonia much the largest, Egypt the most consequential through the Greek version and the Alexandrian school, and Syria the least numerous, whose synagogues were nevertheless the first buildings in which Jesus was preached as Messiah — adding that the scorn of the question was turned by the after history into an unconscious prophecy, like the words of Caiaphas.

Calvin has no doubt that Christ addresses his enemies, ridiculing efforts that must fail because the Father has fixed the time, and turns it into a warning, that Christ is present whenever the gospel calls men to hope, so that a man who disregards the presence loses nothing for Christ but is left a stranger to God.

Clarke says the words went to the common people and not to the officers, reports that the pronoun rendered “unto them” is missing from more than eighty copies and from several fathers, and offers three readings of the dispersion — the Jews of the Greek-speaking empire, the Gentiles themselves, or the ten lost tribes.

debates.question: Whom was Jesus answering in verse 33?

positions.view: His enemies, whose efforts he ridicules because the Father has fixed the time
The common people, not the officers — and the pronoun “unto them” is absent from more than eighty copies
The hierarchy at large; the better manuscripts do omit the pronoun

debates.question: Who are “the dispersed among the Gentiles”?

positions.view: Greeks in the strict sense, or the Jews among them — the distinction between Hebrews and Hellenists is the key
Either the Jews of the Greek-speaking empire, the Gentiles themselves, or the ten lost tribes
Jews scattered in every land, with the question of place turned aside altogether
The historic dispersion of Babylonia, Egypt and Syria, whose synagogues first heard Jesus preached as Messiah

outliers.claim: Cannot find the officers ever laying hold of him, and so has the Pharisees send them not to arrest but to hear him teach.

themes: And many of the people believed on him, and said, When Christ cometh, will he do more miracles than these which this man hath done?
The Pharisees heard that the people murmured such things concerning him; and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to take him.
Then said Jesus unto them, Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go unto him that sent me.
Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come.
Then said the Jews among themselves, Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?
What manner of saying is this that he said, Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come?

37.pericope_label: If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink: out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water

schools.summary: Augustine turns the thirst inward, since the inner man loves more than the outer, so we go to this water not on our feet but on our affections; he makes the belly the conscience of the inner man and the river the love of a neighbour, so that a man who thinks the water given to satisfy himself alone has none flowing from him, while the man who does good to others drinks the whole fountain and becomes it. On the Spirit he grants that the Spirit was with God already and not given to believers until the rising, then faces his own objection, that the Baptist, Zacharias, Mary, Simeon and Anna were filled before: what was new after the exaltation, he answers, was men speaking tongues they had never learned; and asked why nobody speaks all tongues now, he answers that the Church herself speaks the tongues of all nations, so a man outside her does not receive the Spirit while one who loves unity owns whatever anyone in her has. Jerome supplies from the Proverbs the testimony about fountains dispersed abroad which Chrysostom could not find. Alcuin sets the promise before the Ascension and the fiery tongues after.

Chrysostom has the feast over and the people about to go home, so that the cry is provision for the road, and explains the choice of day, since an offer made earlier would have slipped from minds full of the festival; he stresses that no compulsion is used, only a condition of desire, finds no passage that says what the Scripture is said to say and would stop the sentence earlier, making the believing and not the flowing what Scripture prescribed, notes the plural rivers and the word living, meaning always in motion, pointing to the wisdom of Stephen, the tongue of Peter and the strength of Paul, and distinguishes the earlier gift, since the apostles cast out devils by a power given them and not by the Spirit given. Theophylact explains the crying as meant to be heard, giving others confidence.

Lightfoot questions the greatness of the day, since the bullocks diminish through the week until one is left, so that by the count of sacrifices it was the least of them, and supplies the Jewish opinion that the Spirit had departed with Zechariah and Malachi, which is why men at Ephesus could say they had not heard whether there were a Holy Spirit. Barnes gives five reasons for the title, among them the solemn assembly, the finishing of the law and the drawing of water from Siloam, supposes Christ cried while that ceremony went forward to illustrate his doctrine and draw men off a rite never commanded, denies that any one passage of Scripture is meant and takes the substance of the prophets, pointing to the spring whose waters fail not, and makes diffusiveness the nature of piety, so that nobody can believe without desiring the same for others, quoting the Jewish figure of reins that are fountains. Ellicott weighs the seventh day against the eighth and takes the eighth, then turns Barnes’s point over, since on that day the water was not drawn at all and the very absence of the ceremony may be what prompted the declaration of the thing it had signified; he rejects both repunctuations as attempts which, in avoiding the difficulty, also miss the sense, and puts it that every man in living communion with Christ becomes himself a centre of spiritual influence. Robertson insists the words touch the dispensation and not the existence of the Spirit, and takes the clause for the Evangelist’s own comment, written late and pointing to Pentecost.

Calvin takes the plural for the diversified graces of the Spirit and turns it into a rebuke, since graces that would flow like rivers come into us scarcely by drops, faith being too small to receive him.

debates.question: Was the water-drawing ceremony in progress when Jesus cried?

positions.view: Yes — he cried while it went forward, to illustrate his doctrine and draw men off a rite never commanded
No — on the eighth day the water was not drawn at all, and the very absence of the ceremony may be what prompted the declaration
The day’s greatness is itself doubtful, since the sacrifices diminish through the week

debates.question: What Scripture is quoted in “as the scripture hath said”?

positions.view: None that says it — stop the sentence earlier, so that the believing and not the flowing is what Scripture prescribed
The Proverbs on fountains dispersed abroad
No single place, but the substance of the prophets
Neither repunctuation will do; they avoid the difficulty and miss the sense

outliers.claim: Answers why nobody now speaks all tongues by making the Church herself the speaker of every nation’s tongue, so that a man outside her unity receives no Spirit while one who loves unity owns whatever anyone in her has.

themes: In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
(But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.)

40.pericope_label: Of a truth this is the Prophet: shall Christ come out of Galilee? there was a division among the people

schools.summary: Alcuin reads the first two groups as men who had begun to drink the spiritual thirst and laid the unbelieving thirst aside, while the third remained dried up in unbelief; on the failed arrest he gives the reason plainly, that the one who held power over their designs did not permit it.

Chrysostom asks why they argue about the birthplace when the descent was the real question, since they knew he was of the house of David and suppressed his extraction in order to put forward where he had been brought up; had they wanted the truth, he says, they would have gone and asked how the prophets can say Bethlehem while he comes from Galilee, and because they were careless of knowing it he gave them no answer, though he had praised Nathanael for a question of the same shape. He reads the attempted arrest as proof that they had no anxiety to learn anything, and finds the failure of it enough to have raised compunction in any other men, since malignity believes nothing and looks only to blood. Theophylact observes that the division was not among the rulers, who were settled one way, the moderate among them using malicious words to block his path to glory while the more malignant wanted hands laid on him.

Robertson notes that those who named him the Christ went further than those who named him the Prophet, and said it openly. Ellicott raises the question the passage has always provoked, how the Apostle could record such objections without correcting them, and answers that he is giving the feelings and words of the multitude as they really occurred, so that the absence of correction is itself a mark of truthful narrative; he adds that a writer of the second century, with the earlier Gospels before him, could not have made so great a mistake unintentionally nor have thrown himself into the spirit of a Jewish crowd so completely as to invent the question, and separates the Prophet from the Christ in the crowd’s words, as the legates of the Sanhedrin had separated them earlier.

Calvin ranks the three groups in the same order as Alcuin, allowing the second a more correct opinion than the first, and draws the lesson from the quarrel: the schism arose not among Gentiles who were strangers to faith but in the chief seat of the Church, and a man ought not to be distressed at seeing those who wish to be counted God’s people fighting over contrary opinions. The divisions do not come out of the gospel, their seed lying concealed in men beforehand, as vapours are raised by something other than the sun yet appear only when the sun is up; and the peace of men who do not know God arises more from stupidity than from agreement. On the objection he finds the same contempt under the ignorance, since men who had taken the trouble to inquire would have found both titles belonged to him, and remarks how diligent men are in seeking an excuse to turn from Christ and how dull in receiving sound doctrine, so that the Scriptures which lead us to Christ by the hand are made into obstacles.

Clarke turns the objection on the reader: had they examined a little further they would have found the birth exactly as foretold, and many still lose their souls in the same way, led away by common report and refusing a fair hearing, which is the ground on which unbelief has established itself.

debates.question: Why did John record the crowd’s mistake about Galilee without correcting it?

positions.view: Because he gives their words as they really occurred; the absence of correction is itself a mark of truthful narrative, and no second-century writer could have invented it
Because the objectors were careless of knowing, and Christ himself gave them no answer

debates.question: How do the three groups in the crowd rank?

positions.view: The first two had begun to drink and laid unbelief aside; the third remained dried up
Same order, with the second holding a more correct opinion than the first
Those who said “the Christ” went further than those who said “the Prophet”, and said it openly

outliers.claim: Makes the schism a comfort rather than a scandal, since it arose in the chief seat of the Church and its seed lay concealed in men beforehand, as vapours are raised by something other than the sun yet appear only when the sun is up.

themes: Many of the people therefore, when they heard this saying, said, Of a truth this is the Prophet.
Others said, This is the Christ. But some said, Shall Christ come out of Galilee?
Hath not the scripture said, That Christ cometh of the seed of David, and out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was?
So there was a division among the people because of him.
And some of them would have taken him; but no man laid hands on him.

45.pericope_label: Never man spake like this man: doth our law judge any man, before it hear him?

schools.summary: Augustine answers the officers’ saying plainly, that he spoke so because he was both God and man, and hears in the Pharisees’ retort an admission that they were charmed; on the curse he sets the halves against each other, since those ignorant of the law believed on him who gave it while its teachers condemned him. Alcuin agrees the officers were led away, and laudably, having left unbelief for faith.

Chrysostom builds the paragraph on a contrast: the scribes, always near Christ and reading the Scriptures, were not profited but harmed, while the officers, who had none of these advantages, were subdued by a single sermon. He bids us admire their judgment, which asked no signs, since they said never man spoke thus and not never man wrought such miracles, and their boldness before the men who sent them; and he calls the appeal to rank the most foolish thing the Pharisees could have said, the ground of accusation being that the people believed and the rulers did not, so that he asks how men convinced by the law can be the cursed ones.

Robertson quotes the rabbinic maxim that no brutish man is sin-fearing nor any of the people of the earth pious, and on the closing verse is blunter than the rest: the oldest copies omit what follows, it appears first in Codex Bezae, and it is probably a true story because it is like Jesus, but no part of this Gospel. Ellicott sets the people of the earth against the holy people and refuses the reading that makes the curse an excommunication; he catches with Clarke the historical error about Galilee, holds that adverse criticism would charge the mistake to the Evangelist, and calls the following passage one of the most striking instances of an undoubted addition, apostolic in age but not from the pen of John, so that this verse joins the insertion to something we cannot identify. Barnes adds that if the people were ignorant the fault lay with the rulers, whose business was to teach them, marks “art thou also of Galilee” as reproach of the highest kind, and reads the breaking up as disorder, a melancholy exhibition of pride and anger brought to an inquiry, seeing God let their passions dissolve the assembly so that Jesus was safe.

Calvin divides the Pharisees’ pride in two, a tyranny claimed on the title of priests and a contempt of everyone else, which he finds again in priests of his own day who allow none but themselves the name of the Church. On Nicodemus he returns a double verdict: a neutral man who dares not undertake the defence of sound doctrine yet cannot bear to see truth oppressed, so that the mention is partly to his praise and partly to his shame, a spark of godliness shining in his venturing one word while he still hankers after the concealment of night; against those who plead his example he presses that what he says might be said for a robber, and that in saving the person he abandons the doctrine, the better use of the case being that God lets a doctrine take root in secret and bud long after, as this man’s faith gathered vigour from the death of Christ. Of the chapter’s end he says only that the close is astonishing.

Clarke supplies the rabbinic contempt, the people of the earth not thought worthy of a resurrection, and notes that when they paid well they purchased their masters’ good opinion; he catches the historical error about Galilee, Jonah having come from Gath-hepher in Zebulun, and adds that no prophet having arisen from a place is no proof that none could; on the text he reports the next verse and the eleven following wanting in several manuscripts, obelised in others, and carrying a variety of reading found nowhere else in the sacred writings. Wesley puts Nicodemus’s question more kindly, as asking whether the council did not themselves act like men ignorant of the law in sentencing before hearing.

debates.question: How should Nicodemus’s intervention be judged?

positions.view: A double verdict — partly praise, partly shame; his plea might be made for a robber, and in saving the person he abandons the doctrine
More kindly: he asks whether the council were not themselves acting like men ignorant of the law

debates.question: Does John 7:53 belong to this Gospel?

positions.view: Doubtful — wanting in several manuscripts, obelised in others, with a variety of reading found nowhere else in the sacred writings
An undoubted addition, apostolic in age and a real incident, but not from the pen of John
Certainly no part of John: the oldest copies omit it and it appears first in Codex Bezae, though it is probably a true story because it is like Jesus

outliers.claim: Grants the Pharisees’ charge and turns it, saying the officers were indeed led away, and laudably, having left unbelief for faith.

themes: Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him?
The officers answered, Never man spake like this man.
Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived?
Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed.
Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,)
Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee? Search, and look: for out of Galilee ariseth no prophet.
And every man went unto his own house.
